text:
## Observations

1. Each pair uses two distinct mochi, so the answer is at most \(\lfloor N/2\rfloor\).
2. If \(K\) pairs are possible, the \(K\) smallest mochi and the \(K\) largest mochi can form \(K\) pairs by matching them in ascending order.
3. A bottom that is too small for the smallest unmatched top is too small for every remaining top. Using the earliest eligible bottom leaves the most choices for later tops.
4. The input is already sorted. The pairing condition is the integer comparison \(2a \le b\), so a bottom exactly twice the size of its top is valid.

## Solution sketch

> Each pair uses two distinct mochi, so the answer is at most \(\lfloor N/2\rfloor\).

1. Let \(M=\lfloor N/2\rfloor\). Use the first \(M\) mochi as candidates for tops and the remaining \(N-M\) as candidates for bottoms. The two groups are disjoint, including when \(N\) is odd.

> If \(K\) pairs are possible, the \(K\) smallest mochi and the \(K\) largest mochi can form \(K\) pairs by matching them in ascending order.

2. To see why the split preserves an optimum, take any feasible set of \(K\) pairs and sort its tops and bottoms separately. For the \(i\)-th smallest top, the \(K-i+1\) tops at least that large each have a distinct bottom at least twice its size. Thus the \(i\)-th smallest bottom is large enough for that top. Replacing the sorted tops with the \(K\) smallest mochi can only decrease their sizes, and replacing the sorted bottoms with the \(K\) largest can only increase theirs. Since \(K\le M\), these two sets lie in the respective candidate groups.

> A bottom that is too small for the smallest unmatched top is too small for every remaining top. Using the earliest eligible bottom leaves the most choices for later tops.

3. Start a pointer at the beginning of each group and initialize the pair count to zero. If the current bottom is too small, advance only the bottom pointer. Otherwise, count a pair and advance both pointers. For any feasible \(K\), step 2 gives an ordered matching for the first \(K\) tops. For each of those tops, the greedy scan uses a bottom at or before its position in that matching. This follows by induction because the next bottom in the ordered matching is still ahead of the previous greedy choice and is eligible. The scan therefore finds at least \(K\) pairs whenever \(K\) is feasible, and every pair it counts is valid.

> The input is already sorted. The pairing condition is the integer comparison \(2a \le b\), so a bottom exactly twice the size of its top is valid.

4. Use this comparison at each pointer position. Stop when either group is exhausted and print the count, which remains zero if no pair fits. Each pointer moves only forward, so the scan takes \(O(N)\) time and \(O(1)\) auxiliary space beyond the \(O(N)\) storage for the input array.

You are a programming problem planner. Produce a natural-language guide
with exactly these headings:
## Observations
Give numbered, useful observations derived from the problem specification.
## Solution sketch
Describe one coherent algorithm as numbered steps. Before each step quote the
relevant observation exactly, then explain how that observation supports the step.
Cover edge cases and time/space complexity in the sketch.
Return prose only, without Python implementation or command blocks.
The guide will be implemented by a separate coding agent.

isolation.mechanism: codex exec, fresh ephemeral session, empty temporary working directory, user config and exec rules ignored, read-only sandbox, web search and listed features disabled, credential-like variables removed from the environment
isolation.limits: Codex harness instructions and its own tool descriptions remain in the model context; they cannot be removed. Tool isolation is verified post hoc from the event stream, which contained no tool, command, file or search events.
